title: Luke
tagline: The most orderly Gospel: Jesus as Savior for everyone, with a special eye on the poor, outsiders, women, and the lost.
author: Traditionally Luke, a doctor and companion of Paul
authorNote: The book doesn't name its author. Early church tradition says Luke, the doctor Paul mentions (Colossians 4:14), wrote it and Acts as a two-part work addressed to Theophilus. Many scholars accept that; some doubt that the author knew Paul personally.
audience: Theophilus, and through him Gentile and Jewish followers of Jesus
audienceNote: The opening names "most excellent Theophilus," a title of a person of rank. Whether he was a real patron, a new believer, or a symbolic reader ("lover of God") is debated. The Gospel explains Jewish customs and places and stresses that salvation reaches all nations, which suggests a largely Gentile readership.
setting: Under Roman rule, told with careful dates
settingNote: Luke ties the story to Roman and local rulers: Augustus, Quirinius, Tiberius, Pontius Pilate, Herod, and the high priests Annas and Caiaphas. Most scholars date the book to the 70s or 80s AD, after the fall of Jerusalem; some argue for the early 60s. The date is debated.
genreNote: The first half of a two-volume work (Luke and Acts). It opens with a careful preface like an ancient history, and it includes stories found only in Luke, such as the good Samaritan, the prodigal son, and the road to Emmaus.
bigIdea: God has visited his people in Jesus, and the good news of salvation is for everyone, beginning with the lowly and the lost.
themes: Joy and a journey to Jerusalem
mapSummary: Jesus is born in Bethlehem, grows up in Nazareth, teaches in Galilee, journeys toward Jerusalem, and after his resurrection meets two disciples on the road to Emmaus.
